item.title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
item.guid: title:fact checking at scale building a more accurate and efficient synopsis factuality system
item.description: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein . Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in.

item.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
item.guid: title:kimi k3 open frontier intelligence
item.description: Today, we are introducing Kimi K3 — our most capable model. Kimi K3 is a 2. 8T-parameter model built on our Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, with native vision capabilities and a 1-million-token context window. It is the world's first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence across long-horizon coding, knowledge work, and reasoning. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5. 6 Sol, Kimi K3 demonstrated frontier-level performance across our evaluation suite, consistently outperforming other tested models.

item.title: A Decision Model as a Gate: Fast, Well Calibrated, and Still Wrong 16% of the Time
item.guid: title:a decision model as a gate fast well calibrated and still wrong 16 of the time
item.description: Can a small decision model like Jev sit between an agent and its tools in . NET? Here’s what other people measured, what I built to test it myself, and the bar I set before running anything. Why I care about this particular question Most of my agents already have a permission gate. Today it is a mix of allow-lists, a regex or two, and a human who clicks “approve” more often than they would like to admit. The pitch for decision models like Jev is very tempting for exactly that spot: one typed yes/no question, an answer in a few hundred milliseconds, a probability you can put a threshold on, and almost no cost per call.

item.title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
item.guid: title:my ai agent bought me a car
item.description: Sam Herring ’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves? He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.

item.title: Introducing PerceptionBench
item.guid: title:introducing perceptionbench
item.description: Evaluating Atomic Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models Authors Kimi Team We are releasing PerceptionBench , a benchmark that isolates visual perception and evaluates it as a set of atomic capabilities— discovered from how today's models fail, not defined in advance. From frontier-model failures across 42 benchmarks, we derive 10 atomic perceptual capabilities and construct 3,000 verified questions, each isolating a single capability and answerable by looking, with no reasoning or external knowledge required.

item.title: The Interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for AI safety. They seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build.
item.guid: title:the interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for ai safety they seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build
item.description: It’s hard to reason about the safety of neural networks without understanding what happens inside them. Our goal is to be able to explain large language models’ behavior, and to use that understanding to identify problems that are hard to see from the outside, such as situations where a model’s stated reasoning differs from what it’s actually doing. Our early work focused on mapping the internal mechanisms of AI models. Today, we increasingly apply our methods to real models to understand how they think and why they behave the way they do. We’ve developed techniques that allow us to understand models’ inner workings in plain language, making it easier to detect unsafe behavior or dishonest reasoning and safeguard against it. item.title: Know Before You Cut Over: Building a Migration Readiness Checker
item.guid: title:know before you cut over building a migration readiness checker
item.description: Turning platform migration guidance into an automated risk report The problem Many organisations run their applications on an internal developer platform built on top of a public cloud and Kubernetes. The platform gives product teams a paved road: clusters, networking, ingress, monitoring, and security scanning out of the box. Sooner or later, that platform needs a new generation. When it arrives, every product has to move, and the old platform gets a fixed shutdown date. Teams have to migrate while still shipping features. A typical next-generation platform changes how teams own, configure, and secure their workloads: Area Old platform New platform Cloud account A resource group per team A dedicated cloud subscription per team, with more control Management A YAML configuration file in each repo A self-service portal Network & security One shared network Redesigned network; outgoing traffic can be restricted per namespace Ingress ingress-nginx Traefik, since ingress-nginx has been retired by the Kubernetes community Security tooling Trivy vulnerability reports Wiz vulnerability reports The platform team usually publishes a good migration guide.

item.title: A PR bot that cites our own outages
item.guid: title:a pr bot that cites our own outages
item.description: Code review has a blind spot, and it’s history. A reviewer looking at a three-line change to auth/session. py sees three reasonable lines. They don’t see that this file was in the middle of three outages in the last ten weeks, or that the obvious fix for those outages never worked. I built a small bot for DejaVu, my incident-response agent with long-term memory, that puts that history into the pull request. If a PR touches a file with an incident history, the bot comments with every incident that file was part of.
